questions.q: The Earth is best described in shape as:
o: an oblate spheroid (geoid), flattened at the poles
an egg pointed at the poles
questions.why: The Earth bulges slightly at the Equator and is flattened at the poles; its own unique shape is called a geoid.

questions.q: Which layer of gases protects life on Earth from harmful ultraviolet rays of the Sun?
questions.why: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most ultraviolet radiation.

questions.q: Which observation proves that the Earth is round?
o: The Sun rises in the east
The curved shadow of the Earth on the Moon during a lunar eclipse
questions.why: Only a sphere always casts a circular shadow, whatever its position.

questions.q: The Earth's equatorial diameter compared with its polar diameter is:
questions.why: The equatorial diameter is about 12,756 km and the polar diameter about 12,714 km: a difference of about 42 km.

questions.q: When a ship sails towards a port, the first part of it seen from the shore is the:
o: top of the mast or funnel
questions.why: Because the sea surface curves, the top of the ship appears over the horizon before the hull.

long.q: Give three reasons why the Earth is the only known planet that supports life.
scheme: B1: it lies at a suitable distance from the Sun, so its temperature is neither too hot nor too cold
B1: it has an atmosphere with oxygen for breathing and an ozone layer that blocks harmful ultraviolet rays
B1: it has plenty of liquid water, needed by all living things

long.q: Describe three proofs that the Earth is spherical.
scheme: B1: during a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow on the Moon is always curved
B1: a ship approaching the shore shows its mast first and its hull later, because the sea surface is curved

B1: photographs taken from space show a round Earth / travellers such as Magellan's crew sailed round it in one direction and returned to their starting point / the horizon widens as one climbs higher

long.q: Why does the Sun rise at different times at different places on the Earth?
scheme: B1: the Earth is round and rotates from west to east
B1: so places further east face the Sun earlier and see sunrise before places to their west (e.g. sunrise in Arunachal Pradesh is earlier than in Gujarat)

long.q: Explain why the Earth is called the ‘blue planet’, and state two ways in which the hydrosphere supports life.
scheme: B1: about 71% of the Earth's surface is covered by water, so it appears blue from space
B1: water is needed by plants and animals and evaporates to give rain, which supports agriculture
B1: oceans moderate temperature and are home to a vast range of living things

long.q: Describe the shape of the Earth and explain why it is not a perfect sphere.
scheme: B1: the Earth is an oblate spheroid or geoid: slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the Equator
B1: this is because of its rotation, which throws material outward most strongly at the Equator

questions.q: The Tropic of Cancer lies at:
questions.why: The Tropic of Cancer is 23½° N; the Tropic of Capricorn is 23½° S; the Arctic Circle is 66½° N.

questions.q: How much time does the Earth take to turn through 1° of longitude?
questions.why: 360° in 24 hours = 1,440 minutes ÷ 360 = 4 minutes for each degree.

questions.q: Indian Standard Time is based on the meridian of:
questions.why: 82°30′ E, passing near Prayagraj (Mirzapur), gives IST 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.

questions.q: Which of these is a great circle?
questions.why: A great circle divides the Earth into two equal halves; the Equator is the only parallel that does this.

questions.q: A ship crossing the International Date Line from west to east (from Asia towards America):
o: repeats a day, setting the calendar back by one day
changes time by one hour only
questions.why: East of the line is a day behind the west, so travelling eastward the date is put back by one day.

long.q: When it is 12 noon at Greenwich (0°), what is the local time at a place on 75° E? Show your working.
scheme: M1: difference in longitude = 75°; time difference = 75 × 4 minutes = 300 minutes
A1: 300 minutes = 5 hours
A1: the place is east of Greenwich so it is ahead: local time = 12 noon + 5 h = 5 p.m.

long.q: The local time at a place is 7 a.m. when it is 12 noon at Greenwich. Find the longitude of the place. Show your working.
scheme: M1: time difference = 12:00 − 7:00 = 5 hours = 300 minutes
M1: longitude difference = 300 ÷ 4 = 75°
A1: the place's time is behind Greenwich, so it is west: 75° W

long.q: Distinguish between latitude and longitude on three points.
scheme: B1: latitude is the angular distance of a place north or south of the Equator; longitude is the angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian
B1: latitudes range from 0° to 90° N and S; longitudes range from 0° to 180° E and W
B1: parallels of latitude are full circles that get smaller towards the poles; meridians of longitude are semicircles of equal length that meet at the poles

long.q: What is a great circle? Why do ships and aircraft follow great-circle routes?
scheme: B1: a great circle is any circle on the Earth's surface whose plane passes through the centre, dividing the Earth into two equal halves
B1: the shortest distance between two places lies along a great circle, so following it saves time and fuel

long.q: Why does India have one standard time? Why is 82°30′ E chosen as its Standard Meridian?
scheme: B1: India stretches about 30° of longitude, so local times at its east and west ends differ by about 2 hours
B1: one standard time avoids confusion in railway timetables, broadcasts, offices and communication
B1: 82°30′ E runs through about the middle of the country and is a multiple of 7½°, giving IST exactly 5 h 30 min ahead of GMT

questions.q: The Earth rotates on its axis from:
questions.why: Rotation from west to east is why the Sun appears to rise in the east.

questions.q: On which date are the Sun's rays vertical over the Tropic of Capricorn?
questions.why: 22 December is the winter solstice in the northern hemisphere; the Sun is overhead at 23½° S.

questions.q: Day and night are equal all over the world on:
questions.why: At the equinoxes the Sun is overhead at the Equator, and the circle of illumination passes through both poles.

questions.q: The deflection of winds to the right in the northern hemisphere is caused by:
o: the rotation of the Earth (Coriolis force)
questions.why: The Coriolis effect of rotation deflects moving air and water to the right in the north and to the left in the south (Ferrel's law).

questions.q: The Earth's axis is inclined to the plane of its orbit at an angle of:
questions.why: The axis makes 66½° with the orbital plane, which is 23½° from the perpendicular to it.

long.q: State three effects of the rotation of the Earth.
scheme: B1: it causes day and night
B1: it causes a difference of time between places on different longitudes
B1: it deflects winds and ocean currents (Coriolis effect) / it contributes to the daily rise and fall of tides

long.q: Explain how the revolution of the Earth, together with the tilt of its axis, causes seasons.
scheme: B1: the Earth goes round the Sun in about 365¼ days with its axis always tilted in the same direction
B1: so for part of the year the northern hemisphere leans towards the Sun and for part of the year away from it
B1: the hemisphere leaning towards the Sun gets more direct (vertical) rays and longer days, so it has summer
B1: the other hemisphere gets slanting rays and shorter days, so it has winter; this reverses six months later

long.q: What is meant by the summer solstice? State two conditions that occur on that day in the northern hemisphere.
scheme: B1: the summer solstice (21 June) is the day the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer
B1: the northern hemisphere has its longest day and shortest night
B1: places within the Arctic Circle have 24 hours of daylight (the midnight sun)

long.q: What is a leap year and why is it needed?
scheme: B1: a leap year has 366 days, with 29 days in February, every fourth year
B1: the Earth takes about 365¼ days to go round the Sun, so the extra quarter day each year adds up to one day in four years

long.q: Distinguish between perihelion and aphelion.
scheme: B1: perihelion is the position when the Earth is nearest the Sun (about 147 million km), around 3 January
B1: aphelion is the position when the Earth is farthest from the Sun (about 152 million km), around 4 July

topics.name: Structure of the Earth and Landforms

questions.q: The innermost layer of the Earth, made mostly of nickel and iron, is the:
questions.why: The core is called NIFE (nickel + iron); its outer part is liquid and its inner part solid.

questions.q: The continental crust is made mainly of silica and alumina and is called:
questions.why: Sial (Si + Al) is lighter continental crust; sima (Si + Mg) forms the denser ocean floor.

questions.q: The Himalayas are an example of:
questions.why: They were formed by folding of sediments when the Indian plate pushed against the Eurasian plate.

questions.q: The Aravalli range is an example of:
questions.why: The Aravallis are very old mountains that have been worn down by erosion over millions of years.

questions.q: The Tibetan Plateau, surrounded by mountains on all sides, is an example of:
questions.why: An intermontane plateau lies between or is enclosed by mountain ranges.

long.q: Describe the three main layers of the Earth's interior.
scheme: B1: crust: the thin outer layer, thicker under the continents (sial) and thinner under the oceans (sima)
B1: mantle: below the crust to about 2,900 km depth; its upper part (asthenosphere) is semi-molten and is a source of magma
B1: core: the centre, made of nickel and iron (nife), with a liquid outer core and a solid inner core

long.q: Explain how block mountains are formed. Give one example.
scheme: B1: block mountains are formed by faulting, when tension or compression breaks the crust along cracks (faults)
B1: a block of land is raised between two faults (a horst), or the land on either side sinks, leaving the block standing high
B1: example: the Vosges and the Black Forest, with the Rhine rift valley between them / the Satpura range

long.q: How are depositional plains formed? Name two types with an example of each.
scheme: B1: depositional plains are built up by the deposition of material carried by rivers, glaciers or wind
B1: they are usually flat and fertile, and support dense population
B1: alluvial plain: the Indo-Gangetic plain / delta plain: the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta
B1: loess plain: the loess plateau of northern China / glacial or outwash plain: parts of northern Europe

long.q: Distinguish between fold mountains and residual mountains, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: fold mountains are formed when layers of rock are compressed and bent into folds by movements of the crust
B1: example: the Himalayas / Alps / Rockies / Andes
B1: residual mountains are what remains of older high land after long erosion has worn it down
B1: example: the Aravallis / Nilgiris / Eastern Ghats

long.q: State two ways in which plateaus are useful to people.
scheme: B1: plateaus are often rich in minerals, e.g. the Chota Nagpur plateau has coal and iron ore
B1: lava plateaus have fertile black soil good for cotton (Deccan plateau), and plateau edges have waterfalls for hydroelectric power

questions.q: Granite is an example of which type of rock?
questions.why: Granite forms when magma cools slowly deep underground, giving large crystals.

questions.q: Fossils are most commonly found in:
questions.why: Plant and animal remains are buried in layers of sediment and preserved; the heat of igneous rocks destroys them.

questions.q: When limestone is changed by heat and pressure, it becomes:
questions.why: Limestone → marble; sandstone → quartzite; shale → slate; granite → gneiss.

questions.q: Basalt has very fine crystals because:
o: lava cooled quickly at the surface
questions.why: Rapid cooling of lava leaves little time for crystals to grow.

questions.q: Igneous rocks are called primary rocks because:
o: other rocks are formed from them
they are found only at the poles
questions.why: They form first from magma; weathering and metamorphism of them give sedimentary and metamorphic rocks.

long.q: Distinguish between intrusive and extrusive igneous rocks, with one example of each.
scheme: B1: intrusive igneous rocks form when magma cools slowly below the surface
B1: they have large crystals; example: granite
B1: extrusive igneous rocks form when lava cools quickly on the surface
B1: they have small or no crystals; example: basalt

long.q: How are sedimentary rocks formed? State two of their characteristics.
scheme: B1: weathered rock fragments, sand, mud and remains of plants and animals are carried by rivers, wind or ice and deposited, usually in water
B1: over long periods the layers are pressed and cemented together to form rock
B1: they occur in layers (strata)
B1: they may contain fossils and are generally softer and more easily eroded than igneous rocks

long.q: Name the metamorphic rock formed from each of the following: (a) sandstone (b) shale (c) granite.
scheme: B1: sandstone → quartzite
B1: shale → slate
B1: granite → gneiss

long.q: Describe the rock cycle.
scheme: B1: magma cools to form igneous rocks
B1: igneous rocks are weathered and eroded, and the sediments are deposited and hardened into sedimentary rocks
B1: heat and pressure change igneous and sedimentary rocks into metamorphic rocks
B1: metamorphic and other rocks may melt deep in the Earth to form magma again, so the cycle continues

long.q: Distinguish between a mineral and a rock, and state two uses of rocks.
scheme: B1: a mineral is a naturally occurring substance with a definite chemical composition; a rock is an aggregate of one or more minerals
B1: rocks are used for building, e.g. marble (from Makrana) in the Taj Mahal and red sandstone in the Red Fort
B1: rocks weather to form soil, and some rocks contain valuable minerals and fuels such as coal

questions.q: India's only active volcano is on:
questions.why: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea has erupted in recent times; Narcondam is considered dormant.

questions.q: Molten rock material below the Earth's surface is called:
questions.why: It is magma underground and lava once it reaches the surface.

questions.q: A large basin-shaped depression formed when the top of a volcano collapses is a:
questions.why: A caldera is much larger than a crater, which is the small funnel at the top of the vent.

questions.q: About two-thirds of the world's active volcanoes lie along the:
questions.why: The Ring of Fire runs round the edges of the Pacific Ocean, where plates meet.

questions.q: Which Italian volcano buried the town of Pompeii in AD 79?
questions.why: Ash from Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum.

long.q: Classify volcanoes according to their activity, giving one example of each type.
scheme: B1: active volcanoes erupt frequently or have erupted recently, e.g. Mauna Loa, Etna, Stromboli, Barren Island
B1: dormant volcanoes have not erupted for a long time but may erupt again, e.g. Fujiyama, Narcondam
B1: extinct volcanoes are not expected to erupt again, e.g. Mt Popa (Myanmar)

long.q: Name three types of material thrown out during a volcanic eruption.
scheme: B1: liquid: lava
B1: gases: steam, carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and others
B1: solid fragments (pyroclasts): ash, dust, lapilli and volcanic bombs

long.q: State two harmful and two useful effects of volcanoes.
scheme: B1: harmful: lava and ash destroy towns, farms and lives, as at Pompeii
B1: harmful: volcanic gases and ash pollute the air and can disrupt air travel and climate
B1: useful: lava weathers into fertile soil, such as the black soil of the Deccan
B1: useful: volcanic areas provide geothermal energy, hot springs and valuable minerals, and attract tourists

long.q: Explain why volcanoes are found mostly along plate boundaries.
scheme: B1: at plate boundaries the crust is weak and cracked
B1: where plates pull apart or one plate sinks under another, rock melts into magma, which rises through these weak zones to the surface

long.q: Name three volcanic zones of the world.
scheme: B1: the Circum-Pacific belt (Ring of Fire)
B1: the Mid-Atlantic belt (e.g. Iceland)
B1: the Mediterranean belt (e.g. Vesuvius, Etna) / the East African Rift

questions.q: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the origin of an earthquake is the:
questions.why: The focus (hypocentre) is underground; the epicentre is directly above it, where shaking is usually strongest.

questions.q: Which seismic waves cannot pass through liquids?
questions.why: S waves are transverse and stop at the liquid outer core; P waves travel through solids and liquids.

questions.q: The magnitude of an earthquake is measured on the:
questions.why: The Richter scale measures energy released (magnitude); the Mercalli scale measures intensity from observed damage.

questions.q: The Bhuj earthquake that devastated Kachchh took place on:
questions.why: It struck Gujarat on Republic Day, 26 January 2001; Latur (Maharashtra) was in 1993.

questions.q: A huge sea wave caused by an earthquake on the ocean floor is called a:
questions.why: The 26 December 2004 tsunami, caused by an earthquake off Sumatra, struck India's eastern coast and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

long.q: State three causes of earthquakes.
scheme: B1: movement of tectonic plates, which builds up stress that is released suddenly along faults
B1: volcanic eruptions, which shake the surrounding crust
B1: human activities such as building large dams and reservoirs (e.g. Koyna, 1967) or mining

long.q: Distinguish between P waves, S waves and L waves.
scheme: B1: P (primary) waves are the fastest, reach first, and travel through solids, liquids and gases
B1: S (secondary) waves are slower, move the ground at right angles to their direction, and travel only through solids
B1: L (surface) waves travel along the surface, arrive last and cause the most damage

long.q: State four effects of a severe earthquake.
scheme: B1: buildings, bridges and roads collapse, causing heavy loss of life
B1: landslides in hilly areas and cracks in the ground
B1: tsunamis when the epicentre is under the sea, flooding coasts
B1: fires from broken gas and power lines, and disruption of water supply, leading to disease

long.q: Name two major earthquake belts of the world.
scheme: B1: the Circum-Pacific belt (around the Pacific Ocean)
B1: the Mid-Continental / Mediterranean-Himalayan belt (from the Alps through the Himalayas to South-East Asia) / the Mid-Atlantic ridge

long.q: Suggest three measures that can reduce loss of life and property in earthquake-prone areas.
scheme: B1: constructing earthquake-resistant buildings with flexible frames and following building codes
B1: avoiding heavy construction and large dams in highly active zones, and using light building materials
B1: training people in safety drills (drop, cover, hold) and keeping disaster-response teams ready

questions.q: The peeling off of rock layers like the skin of an onion, common in hot deserts, is called:
questions.why: Heating by day and cooling by night make the outer layers expand and contract until they peel away.

questions.q: Which type of weathering forms caves in limestone areas?
questions.why: Rainwater containing carbon dioxide forms a weak acid that dissolves limestone.

questions.q: An ox-bow lake is formed in the:
o: middle or lower course of a river, when a meander is cut off
questions.why: As a meander loop narrows, the river cuts across its neck in a flood and leaves the old loop as a lake.

questions.q: A crescent-shaped sand dune is called a:
questions.why: Barchans have horns pointing downwind; they are common in hot deserts.

questions.q: Denudation includes:
questions.why: Denudation is the overall wearing down of the land surface by all these processes.

long.q: Distinguish between weathering and erosion.
scheme: B1: weathering is the breaking down of rocks in their original place (in situ) by physical, chemical or biological processes
B1: erosion is the wearing away and removal of rock material by moving agents such as rivers, wind, glaciers and waves

long.q: Explain two types of physical weathering and the climate in which each is common.
scheme: B1: exfoliation / block disintegration: repeated heating and cooling makes rocks expand and contract and break up
B1: it is common in hot deserts with a large daily range of temperature
B1: frost action: water in cracks freezes, expands and forces the rock apart
B1: it is common in cold mountains and high latitudes, where temperatures go above and below freezing

long.q: Name and briefly explain three landforms made by a river in its upper course.
scheme: B1: V-shaped valley: formed by rapid downward cutting of the river bed
B1: gorge or canyon: a very deep, narrow valley with steep sides, e.g. the Grand Canyon of the Colorado
B1: waterfall: formed where the river flows over a band of hard rock lying above softer rock that is worn away, e.g. Jog Falls on the Sharavathi

long.q: How is a delta formed? Why do some rivers not form deltas?
scheme: B1: near its mouth a river slows down and deposits its load of silt, which builds up into a triangular low plain cut by distributaries (e.g. the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta)
B1: deltas form where the sea is shallow and the tides and currents are weak, so the silt is not carried away
B1: rivers like the Narmada and Tapi form estuaries instead, because they flow through rocky beds with little load and their mouths face strong tidal action

long.q: Describe two landforms produced by the action of wind in deserts.
scheme: B1: mushroom rock: wind carrying sand erodes the lower part of a rock more than the top, leaving a rock shaped like a mushroom
B1: sand dunes such as barchans: mounds of sand deposited by wind / loess: fine dust deposited over large areas, e.g. northern China

questions.q: Spring tides occur when:
o: the Sun and Moon are at right angles to the Earth
the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line
questions.why: At new moon and full moon the pulls of Sun and Moon combine, giving the highest high tides.

questions.q: The time between two successive high tides at a place is about:
questions.why: The Moon returns over a place every 24 h 52 min, so high tides come about every 12 h 26 min.

questions.q: The North Atlantic Drift keeps the ports of which country ice-free in winter?
questions.why: This warm current, an extension of the Gulf Stream, warms the coasts of north-west Europe.

questions.q: The cold current that meets the Gulf Stream off Newfoundland is the:
questions.why: The meeting of warm and cold water causes fog and creates the rich Grand Banks fishing ground.

questions.q: The warm Kuroshio meets the cold Oyashio near:
questions.why: Their meeting off Japan creates a rich fishing ground.

long.q: Explain the causes of tides.
scheme: B1: tides are the regular rise and fall of sea level, caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the Moon, and partly of the Sun
B1: the water on the side of the Earth facing the Moon is pulled towards it, forming a high tide
B1: on the opposite side, the centrifugal force due to the rotation of the Earth-Moon system causes a second high tide; low tides occur in between

long.q: Distinguish between spring tides and neap tides.
scheme: B1: spring tides occur on new moon and full moon days
B1: the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line, so their pulls combine and tides are very high
B1: neap tides occur in the first and last quarters of the Moon
B1: the Sun and Moon are at right angles to the Earth, so their pulls partly cancel and the tidal range is smallest

long.q: State three uses of tides.
scheme: B1: high tides help large ships enter shallow harbours and river ports such as Kolkata
B1: the ebb tide carries away silt and waste, keeping harbours clean
B1: tides can be used to generate tidal energy, e.g. in the Gulf of Khambhat / they help fishing

long.q: State three causes of ocean currents.
scheme: B1: planetary winds, such as the trade winds and westerlies, push the surface water
B1: differences in temperature and salinity of sea water make denser water sink and lighter water move
B1: the rotation of the Earth deflects currents (to the right in the northern hemisphere); the shape of coastlines also changes their direction

long.q: Explain how ocean currents affect the climate and economy of coastal lands. Give one example each of a warm and a cold current's effect.
scheme: B1: warm currents raise the temperature of the coasts they pass and bring moisture, so winters are milder
B1: example: the North Atlantic Drift keeps the ports of Norway and Britain ice-free in winter
B1: cold currents lower temperatures and make the air dry, helping form deserts on western coasts
B1: example: the cold Humboldt (Peru) Current helps form the Atacama Desert; where warm and cold currents meet, rich fishing grounds and fog occur

questions.q: Which gas makes up about 78% of the atmosphere?
questions.why: Nitrogen is about 78%, oxygen about 21%, and argon about 0.9%; carbon dioxide is only about 0.04%.

questions.q: In which layer of the atmosphere do almost all weather changes take place?
questions.why: The troposphere contains nearly all the water vapour and dust, so clouds, rain and storms form there.

questions.q: Radio waves are reflected back to the Earth by the:
questions.why: The ionosphere, in the thermosphere, has electrically charged particles that reflect radio waves.

questions.q: Which international agreement of 1987 aimed to phase out ozone-depleting chemicals?
questions.why: The Montreal Protocol phased out CFCs; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and Paris Agreement (2015) deal with greenhouse gases.

questions.q: In the troposphere, temperature normally falls with height at about:
questions.why: This normal lapse rate is why hill stations such as Shimla are cooler than the plains.

long.q: State three characteristics of the troposphere.
scheme: B1: it is the lowest layer, extending to about 8 km at the poles and about 18 km at the Equator
B1: temperature falls with height at about 6.5 °C per km
B1: it contains almost all the water vapour and dust, so all weather phenomena (clouds, rain, storms) occur in it

long.q: Why is the stratosphere important? Explain the role of the ozone layer.
scheme: B1: the stratosphere lies above the troposphere, to about 50 km, and is free of clouds and storms, so jet aircraft fly in its lower part
B1: it contains the ozone layer, which absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation
B1: without it, ultraviolet rays would cause skin cancer, eye damage and harm to plants and animals

long.q: What causes depletion of the ozone layer? State two effects.
scheme: B1: chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) used in old refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays release chlorine that destroys ozone
B1: other chemicals such as halons (in fire extinguishers) also damage it, and an ‘ozone hole’ appears over Antarctica
B1: effect: more ultraviolet radiation reaches the Earth, causing skin cancer and cataracts
B1: effect: damage to crops, plankton and other living things, and weakened immunity

long.q: What is global warming? State three of its effects.
scheme: B1: global warming is the rise in the Earth's average temperature, caused by increasing greenhouse gases (carbon dioxide, methane and others) from burning fossil fuels and deforestation
B1: melting of glaciers and polar ice, causing sea levels to rise and threatening low-lying coasts and islands
B1: changes in rainfall patterns, more droughts, floods and stronger cyclones
B1: harm to agriculture and to plants and animals that cannot adapt

long.q: Name the layers of the atmosphere in order from the Earth's surface upwards.
scheme: B1: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere
B1: thermosphere (including the ionosphere), exosphere

questions.q: Insolation means:
o: heat given off by the Earth
incoming solar radiation received by the Earth
questions.why: It is short for incoming solar radiation.

questions.q: The atmosphere is heated mainly:
o: directly by the Sun's rays from above
from below, by heat radiated from the Earth's surface
questions.why: The air lets most short-wave sunlight through; the warmed ground then radiates long-wave heat that the air absorbs.

questions.q: A town at sea level has a temperature of 32 °C. Using a lapse rate of 6.5 °C per 1,000 m, what is the expected temperature on a hill 2,000 m above it?
Why does Mumbai have a smaller annual range of temperature than Delhi?
o: Mumbai is at a higher altitude
Mumbai is on the coast, and the sea moderates its temperature
questions.why: Places near the sea have a maritime (equable) climate; inland places like Delhi have a continental (extreme) climate.

questions.q: Lines joining places with the same temperature are called:
questions.why: Isobars join equal pressure, isohyets equal rainfall and contours equal height.

long.q: Explain how latitude affects temperature.
scheme: B1: near the Equator the Sun's rays fall almost vertically, so the heat is concentrated on a small area
B1: towards the poles the rays fall slanting, spread over a larger area, and pass through more of the atmosphere
B1: so temperature generally decreases from the Equator towards the poles

long.q: Give reasons why temperature decreases with altitude.
scheme: B1: the atmosphere is heated mainly from below by radiation from the Earth's surface, so places higher up are farther from this source
B1: air at higher levels is thinner and has less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs and holds less heat
B1: so temperature falls by about 6.5 °C for every 1,000 m rise, e.g. Shimla is cooler than Delhi

long.q: Distinguish between maritime and continental climates, giving one Indian example of each.
scheme: B1: a maritime (equable) climate is found near the sea; the sea heats and cools slowly, so summers are not very hot and winters not very cold
B1: example: Mumbai / Chennai / Kochi
B1: a continental (extreme) climate is found far inland, with very hot summers and cold winters and a large annual range
B1: example: Delhi / Amritsar / Kanpur

long.q: State four factors, other than latitude and altitude, that affect the temperature of a place.
scheme: B1: distance from the sea
B1: ocean currents that wash the coast (warm or cold)
B1: prevailing winds blowing from warm or cold regions
B1: cloud cover, slope and aspect of the land, or nature of the ground surface (e.g. sand heats faster than vegetation)

long.q: What is the heat budget of the Earth? Why does the Earth not keep getting hotter?
scheme: B1: the heat budget is the balance between the solar energy the Earth receives (insolation) and the energy it loses back to space
B1: the Earth radiates back as much heat as it receives over time (as terrestrial radiation and reflection), so its average temperature stays nearly the same

questions.q: The trade winds blow from:
o: the sub-polar lows to the poles
the poles to the sub-tropical highs
the sub-tropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low
questions.why: They blow towards the Equator; deflected by rotation they are the north-east trades in the north and south-east trades in the south.

questions.q: The ‘Roaring Forties’ are strong:
questions.why: Over the open southern oceans near 40° S the westerlies blow with great force.

questions.q: A sea breeze blows:
o: from land to sea at night
from sea to land during the day
questions.why: By day the land heats faster, forming low pressure, so cooler air moves in from the sea.

questions.q: A warm, dry wind that descends the eastern slopes of the Rockies and melts snow is the:
questions.why: The Chinook (‘snow eater’) helps the early grazing of cattle on the prairies.

questions.q: In the northern hemisphere, winds in a cyclone blow:
questions.why: In a cyclone, air moves inward and is deflected to the right, giving anticlockwise winds in the north.

long.q: Name the pressure belts of the Earth from the Equator to the North Pole.
scheme: B1: equatorial low-pressure belt (doldrums), about 5° N to 5° S
B1: sub-tropical high-pressure belt (horse latitudes), about 30° to 35° N
B1: sub-polar low-pressure belt, about 60° to 65° N
B1: polar high-pressure belt at the pole

long.q: Explain the formation of land and sea breezes.
scheme: B1: by day the land heats faster than the sea, so the air above it rises and pressure falls
B1: cool air from the sea (higher pressure) blows towards the land: the sea breeze
B1: at night the land cools faster than the sea, so pressure over land becomes higher
B1: air then blows from the land to the sea: the land breeze

long.q: State Ferrel's law and explain its effect on the planetary winds.
scheme: B1: Ferrel's law: winds are deflected to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern hemisphere, because of the Earth's rotation
B1: so the trade winds blow from the north-east in the northern hemisphere and from the south-east in the southern hemisphere
B1: and the westerlies blow from the south-west in the northern hemisphere and from the north-west in the southern hemisphere

long.q: Name the local wind described in each case: (a) a hot, dry wind of north India in May and June (b) a cold wind blowing down the Rhône valley in France (c) a dry, dusty wind of West Africa called the ‘doctor’.
scheme: B1: (a) Loo
B1: (b) Mistral
B1: (c) Harmattan

long.q: Distinguish between a cyclone and an anticyclone.
scheme: B1: a cyclone has low pressure at the centre, while an anticyclone has high pressure at the centre
B1: in a cyclone winds blow inward, anticlockwise in the northern hemisphere; in an anticyclone winds blow outward, clockwise in the northern hemisphere
B1: cyclones bring cloudy, stormy and rainy weather; anticyclones bring calm, clear and dry weather

questions.q: Relative humidity is expressed as:
questions.why: It is the amount of water vapour present compared with the maximum the air could hold at that temperature, × 100.

questions.q: The temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins is the:
questions.why: If air cools below its dew point, water vapour condenses into dew, fog or cloud.

questions.q: Heavy rain on the windward slopes of the Western Ghats is an example of:
questions.why: Moist monsoon winds are forced to rise over the Ghats, cool and give heavy rain; the leeward side is a rain-shadow area.

questions.q: Afternoon thunderstorms every day in equatorial regions are an example of:
questions.why: Intense heating makes moist air rise, cool and form cumulonimbus clouds.

questions.q: Which instrument measures relative humidity?
questions.why: The difference between the wet and dry bulb readings is used to find relative humidity.

long.q: Distinguish between absolute humidity and relative humidity.
scheme: B1: absolute humidity is the actual amount of water vapour in a given volume of air, measured in grams per cubic metre
B1: relative humidity is the ratio of the water vapour actually present to the maximum the air can hold at that temperature, expressed as a percentage

long.q: Explain how orographic rainfall occurs, and what is meant by a rain-shadow area. Give an Indian example.
scheme: B1: moist winds blowing from the sea are forced to rise when they meet a mountain barrier
B1: as they rise they cool, water vapour condenses and heavy rain falls on the windward slope
B1: after crossing the mountain the winds descend, become warmer and drier, and give little rain: this leeward side is the rain-shadow area
B1: example: Mumbai on the windward side of the Western Ghats gets heavy rain, while Pune on the leeward side gets much less

long.q: Describe convectional rainfall and state where it is common.
scheme: B1: the ground is strongly heated, so warm moist air rises in convection currents
B1: the air cools as it rises, condenses into tall cumulonimbus clouds and gives heavy showers with thunder and lightning, usually in the afternoon
B1: it is common in equatorial regions, and in summer in other hot areas

long.q: Name four forms of condensation.
scheme: B1: dew: water droplets on cool surfaces such as grass at night
B1: frost: condensation below 0 °C, forming ice crystals
B1: fog or mist: tiny water droplets suspended in the air near the ground
B1: clouds: masses of water droplets or ice crystals high in the air

long.q: How does cyclonic (frontal) rainfall occur in temperate regions?
scheme: B1: warm, light air masses meet cold, dense air masses along a front
B1: the warm air is forced to rise over the cold air, cools, and gives steady rain over a wide area

questions.q: Acid rain is caused mainly by:
questions.why: These gases from burning coal and oil dissolve in rain to form sulphuric and nitric acids.

questions.q: Noise is measured in:
questions.why: Sound levels are measured in decibels (dB); prolonged noise above about 80-85 dB can damage hearing.

questions.q: The excessive growth of algae in ponds due to fertiliser run-off is called:
questions.why: Nutrients feed algae, which use up oxygen when they decay, killing fish.

questions.q: The nuclear accident at Chernobyl in 1986 is an example of:
questions.why: Radioactive material released from the reactor spread over large parts of Europe.

questions.q: Which disease is caused by drinking water contaminated with sewage?
questions.why: Cholera, typhoid and jaundice spread through polluted water.

long.q: State three sources of air pollution and three effects of air pollution on health.
scheme: B1: sources: smoke from vehicles and factories, burning of coal in thermal power stations, and burning of crop stubble or garbage
B1: effects: respiratory diseases such as asthma and bronchitis, and lung cancer
B1: effects: irritation of the eyes and throat, and heart diseases

long.q: Explain how acid rain is formed and state two of its harmful effects.
scheme: B1: sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides are released by burning coal and petroleum
B1: they dissolve in water vapour in the air to form sulphuric and nitric acids, which fall as acid rain
B1: it damages buildings and monuments of marble and limestone, e.g. the yellowing of the Taj Mahal
B1: it makes lakes and soils acidic, killing fish and harming forests and crops

long.q: Suggest four measures to reduce water pollution.
scheme: B1: treating sewage in treatment plants before it is discharged into rivers
B1: treating industrial effluents before release and enforcing strict laws
B1: using less chemical fertiliser and pesticide so that run-off is reduced
B1: not dumping waste, plastics or idols in rivers, and supporting cleaning programmes such as Namami Gange

long.q: State two sources and two effects of noise pollution.
scheme: B1: source: traffic, horns and aircraft
B1: source: loudspeakers, firecrackers and machines in factories and construction sites
B1: effect: temporary or permanent loss of hearing
B1: effect: stress, sleeplessness, high blood pressure and loss of concentration

long.q: What is soil pollution? State two of its causes.
scheme: B1: soil pollution is the presence of harmful substances in the soil that reduce its fertility and harm living things
B1: excessive use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides
B1: dumping of industrial waste, plastics and mining waste on land

questions.q: Which natural region has hot, wet weather throughout the year with rain almost every afternoon?
questions.why: Near the Equator high temperature all year causes convectional rain; the annual range of temperature is only about 2-3 °C.

questions.q: The Mediterranean climate has:
o: hot, dry summers and mild, wet winters
questions.why: In winter the westerlies bring rain; in summer the region lies under the dry trade-wind belt.

questions.q: The coniferous forests of the Taiga supply mainly:
questions.why: Pine, fir and spruce give soft, light wood used for pulp, paper and timber.

questions.q: The temperate grasslands of Argentina are called the:
questions.why: Prairies (North America), Steppes (Eurasia), Pampas (Argentina), Veld (South Africa), Downs (Australia).

questions.q: The Inuit (Eskimos) live in the:
questions.why: They live in the cold Arctic Tundra, traditionally hunting seals with harpoons from kayaks.

long.q: Describe the climate and natural vegetation of the equatorial region.
scheme: B1: temperatures are high (about 27 °C) all year, with a very small annual range
B1: rainfall is heavy (over 200 cm), mostly convectional, and occurs throughout the year
B1: the vegetation is dense evergreen rainforest, in several layers, with a thick canopy
B1: trees are hardwoods such as mahogany, ebony and rosewood, with many climbers

long.q: How have people adapted to life in hot deserts? Give three ways.
scheme: B1: many are nomads (e.g. Bedouins of Arabia, Tuaregs of the Sahara) who move with their camels, goats and sheep in search of water and pasture
B1: they wear loose, long garments and cover their heads to protect themselves from heat, sun and sandstorms
B1: settled people live in oases, growing date palms and crops with well or spring water

long.q: Why is the Mediterranean region called the ‘orchard of the world’? Name two other areas with this climate.
scheme: B1: the hot sunny summers and mild wet winters suit fruit such as grapes, citrus fruits, olives and figs, grown widely for export and wine
B1: Central California (USA) / central Chile
B1: South-west Australia (around Perth) / the Cape Province of South Africa

long.q: Describe the natural vegetation and animal life of the tropical grassland (savanna).
scheme: B1: tall, coarse grass (elephant grass) grows in the wet season and dries in the dry season
B1: scattered trees such as acacia and baobab, which store water and resist drought
B1: large herds of grazing animals (zebras, giraffes, antelopes) and predators such as lions live there

long.q: State three characteristics of the Tundra region.
scheme: B1: it lies mainly north of the Arctic Circle, with long, very cold winters and a short cool summer
B1: the subsoil is permanently frozen (permafrost), so trees cannot grow; only mosses, lichens and small shrubs grow in summer
B1: population is sparse; people such as the Inuit and the Sami live by hunting, fishing and herding reindeer

questions.q: On a Survey of India map with a scale of 1:50,000, 1 cm on the map represents:
questions.why: 50,000 cm = 500 m = 0.5 km, so 2 cm represent 1 km.

questions.q: Contour lines that are close together show:
questions.why: Closely spaced contours mean height changes over a short distance; widely spaced ones mean a gentle slope.

questions.q: On Survey of India topographical sheets, contours are drawn in:
questions.why: Brown is used for contours and relief, blue for water, green for woodland, yellow for cultivated land.

questions.q: In a four-figure grid reference, the first two figures give the:
questions.why: Eastings (vertical lines, numbered from west to east) are read first, then northings.

questions.q: A V-shaped set of contours with the V pointing towards higher ground shows a:
questions.why: Contours in a valley point upstream, towards higher land; in a spur they point towards lower land.

long.q: On a topographical map with a scale of 1:50,000, two villages are 7.5 cm apart in a straight line. Calculate the actual distance between them in kilometres.
scheme: M1: 1 cm represents 0.5 km, so distance = 7.5 × 0.5

long.q: A forest on a 1:50,000 map covers 6 complete grid squares and about half of 4 other squares. Each grid square has sides of 2 cm. Find the approximate area of the forest.
scheme: M1: 2 cm on the map = 1 km, so each grid square = 1 km × 1 km = 1 km²
M1: area = 6 full squares + 4 half squares = 6 + 2 = 8 squares
A1: approximate area = 8 km²

long.q: A triangulated height on a map reads 412 and a spot height in a nearby village reads 286. Find the difference in height, and explain the difference between a triangulated height and a bench mark.
scheme: B1: difference = 412 − 286 = 126 m
B1: a triangulated height is a height above sea level fixed by survey at a triangulation station, shown by a small triangle with the value
B1: a bench mark is a surveyed height marked on a permanent object such as a building or pillar, shown as BM with its value

long.q: In a map extract, a village lies in the square bounded by easting lines 45 and 46 and northing lines 23 and 24. A temple in it lies 3 tenths of the way east from easting 45 and 7 tenths of the way north from northing 23. Give (a) the four-figure grid reference of the square, (b) the six-figure grid reference of the temple.
scheme: B1: (a) 4523 (the easting of the western line first, then the northing of the southern line)

long.q: A map extract shows many small streams joining a main river like the branches of a tree, a canal with a straight course, and houses clustered along a metalled road. Identify the drainage pattern and settlement pattern, and state what the canal suggests.
scheme: B1: the drainage pattern is dendritic (tree-like)
B1: the settlement pattern is linear, as houses lie along the road
B1: the canal (man-made, straight) suggests that rainfall is not enough or seasonal, and irrigation is needed for agriculture

questions.q: The Tropic of Cancer does NOT pass through which of these states?
questions.why: It passes through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram, but not Bihar.

questions.q: The highest peak in India (excluding K2) is:
questions.why: Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) lies on the Sikkim-Nepal border.

questions.q: Which pass connects Sikkim with Tibet?
questions.why: Nathu La is in Sikkim; Shipki La is in Himachal Pradesh, Zoji La links Srinagar and Ladakh, Bomdi La is in Arunachal Pradesh.

questions.q: The highest peak of South India, Anaimudi, is in the:
questions.why: Anaimudi (2,695 m) is in the Anamalai Hills of Kerala; Doda Betta is the highest peak of the Nilgiris.

questions.q: Chilika Lake, a brackish-water lagoon, is located in:
questions.why: Chilika is on the Odisha coast; Wular (J&K) is a freshwater lake, Sambhar (Rajasthan) a salt lake, Vembanad in Kerala.

long.q: On an outline map of India, a student must mark the Standard Meridian. State its value and name any three states it passes through.
scheme: B1: Uttar Pradesh
B1: Madhya Pradesh / Chhattisgarh
B1: Odisha / Andhra Pradesh (any one further correct state)

long.q: Name the water body described in each case: (a) the gulf between Saurashtra and the mainland of Gujarat near Bharuch and Surat, (b) the strait separating India from Sri Lanka, (c) the lagoon on the Andhra Pradesh-Tamil Nadu border.
scheme: B1: (a) Gulf of Khambhat
B1: (b) Palk Strait
B1: (c) Pulicat Lake
long.ans: Gulf of Khambhat; Palk Strait; Pulicat Lake

long.q: Name one important area for each: (a) petroleum off the Maharashtra coast, (b) coal in the Damodar valley, (c) iron ore in Chhattisgarh, (d) lignite in Tamil Nadu.
scheme: B1: (a) Mumbai High
B1: (b) Jharia / Raniganj / Bokaro
B1: (c) Bailadila
B1: (d) Neyveli

long.q: Describe in words where the following are found: (a) the Thar Desert, (b) the Eastern Ghats, (c) the Palghat Gap.
scheme: B1: (a) the Thar Desert lies in western Rajasthan, west of the Aravallis, extending into Pakistan
B1: (b) the Eastern Ghats run as broken hills along the eastern side of the peninsula, from Odisha through Andhra Pradesh into Tamil Nadu
B1: (c) the Palghat Gap is a gap in the Western Ghats between the Nilgiris and the Anamalai Hills, linking Kerala and Tamil Nadu

long.q: On an outline map, arrows would show the two branches of the south-west monsoon. Name the branches and the region each reaches first.
scheme: B1: the Arabian Sea branch, which first reaches the Kerala coast and the Western Ghats
B1: the Bay of Bengal branch, which first reaches the north-east (Meghalaya, Assam) and West Bengal, and then turns west along the Ganga plain

topics.name: Location, Extent and Physical Features of India

questions.q: The mainland of India extends between the latitudes of about:
questions.why: The mainland lies between about 8°4′ N and 37°6′ N, and 68°7′ E and 97°25′ E.

questions.q: The northernmost range of the Himalayas, with the highest peaks, is the:
questions.why: The Himadri has peaks such as Kanchenjunga; the Himachal is the middle range and the Shiwaliks the outermost foothills.

questions.q: The newer alluvium of the northern plains, renewed by floods every year, is called:
questions.why: Khadar is new, fertile alluvium in floodplains; bhangar is older alluvium on higher ground.

questions.q: The Lakshadweep Islands are:
o: volcanic islands in the Bay of Bengal
coral islands in the Arabian Sea
questions.why: Lakshadweep is made of coral atolls; the Andaman and Nicobar Islands in the Bay of Bengal are mostly raised parts of submerged mountains.

questions.q: The western coastal plain between Goa and Mangaluru is called the:
questions.why: From north to south: Konkan (Mumbai to Goa), Kanara, and Malabar (Kerala); the Coromandel coast is in the east.

long.q: Explain how the Himalayas influence the climate of India.
scheme: B1: they block the cold, dry winds from Central Asia in winter, keeping north India warmer
B1: they act as a barrier to the south-west monsoon winds, forcing them to rise and give heavy rain over the northern plains and the north-east
B1: they are a source of perennial rivers fed by glaciers and snow

long.q: Distinguish between the bhabar and the terai.
scheme: B1: bhabar is a narrow belt of pebbles and coarse gravel along the foot of the Shiwaliks, where streams sink underground
B1: terai lies south of the bhabar; the streams re-emerge and make it marshy and thickly forested

long.q: State three differences between the western and eastern coastal plains.
scheme: B1: the western coastal plain is narrow; the eastern coastal plain is broad
B1: rivers on the west coast are short and swift and form estuaries; rivers on the east coast (Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) form large deltas
B1: the west coast has more natural harbours (Mumbai, Mormugao, Kochi); the east coast is smoother with fewer natural harbours

long.q: State four features of the Peninsular plateau.
scheme: B1: it is the oldest landmass of India, made of ancient hard crystalline rocks
B1: it is bounded by the Aravallis in the north-west, the Western Ghats in the west and the Eastern Ghats in the east
B1: its north-western part (the Deccan trap) is covered by lava, which weathered into black soil
B1: it is rich in minerals such as iron ore, coal and manganese, and slopes generally towards the east, so most rivers flow east

long.q: Give two reasons why the northern plains are densely populated.
scheme: B1: they have fertile alluvial soil deposited by the Ganga, Indus and Brahmaputra systems, good for agriculture
B1: the land is flat and the rivers are perennial, which makes irrigation, transport and building of towns easy

questions.q: Winter rain in Punjab and Haryana, useful for the wheat crop, is brought by:
questions.why: Western disturbances are low-pressure systems from the Mediterranean region that bring winter rain to north-west India.

questions.q: Which part of India receives most of its rainfall from the retreating (north-east) monsoon in October-December?
questions.why: The winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and bring rain to the Tamil Nadu coast.

questions.q: Pre-monsoon showers in Kerala and Karnataka that help the ripening of mangoes are called:
questions.why: Thunderstorms in April-May on the Kerala-Karnataka coast are called mango showers; cherry blossoms help coffee in Karnataka.

questions.q: Mawsynram receives very heavy rainfall because:
o: it lies in the rain shadow
it is on the Thar Desert edge
moist Bay of Bengal winds are trapped and forced to rise over the funnel-shaped Khasi Hills
it lies on the Tropic of Cancer
questions.why: The Garo-Khasi hills force the winds to rise steeply, giving orographic rain.

questions.q: Nor'westers (Kalbaisakhi) in West Bengal and Assam are useful for:
questions.why: These April-May thunderstorms bring rain that helps the tea, jute and rice crops.

long.q: State four factors that affect the climate of India.
scheme: B1: latitude: the Tropic of Cancer divides India into a tropical south and sub-tropical north
B1: the Himalayas, which block cold northern winds and trap the monsoon winds
B1: distance from the sea, which makes coastal areas equable and inland areas extreme
B1: the monsoon winds, relief (Western Ghats), altitude, jet streams or western disturbances (any one)

long.q: Explain the mechanism of the south-west monsoon.
scheme: B1: in summer the land of north-west India becomes very hot, creating an intense low-pressure area
B1: the Indian Ocean is cooler and has higher pressure, so winds blow from the sea towards the land
B1: the south-east trade winds cross the Equator and are deflected to the right, becoming south-west winds
B1: these moist winds, in two branches (Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal), bring most of India's rain from June to September

long.q: Give reasons: (a) Chennai gets rain in winter. (b) Rajasthan receives little rainfall. (c) The west coast receives heavier rain than the Deccan plateau.
scheme: B1: (a) the north-east (retreating) monsoon winds blow over the Bay of Bengal, pick up moisture and bring rain to the Coromandel coast
B1: (b) the Aravallis run parallel to the Arabian Sea branch, so the winds are not forced to rise, and the Bay of Bengal branch has lost its moisture by the time it reaches Rajasthan
B1: (c) the Western Ghats force the Arabian Sea winds to rise and shed rain on the windward west coast, while the Deccan lies in the rain shadow

long.q: Describe the conditions of the hot weather season (March to May) in north India.
scheme: B1: temperatures rise steadily, often exceeding 45 °C in the north-west, as the Sun moves overhead towards the Tropic of Cancer
B1: a low-pressure area develops over north-west India, and hot, dry winds called the Loo blow in the afternoons
B1: dust storms occur in Rajasthan and Punjab, while local thunderstorms bring some relief in the east (Kalbaisakhi)

long.q: What is meant by ‘break in the monsoon’? State one effect.
scheme: B1: a break in the monsoon is a dry spell of a week or more during the rainy season, when rain stops over large areas
B1: it can cause drought conditions and harm crops sown with the monsoon, such as rice

questions.q: Black soil is formed from:
questions.why: Black (regur) soil developed on the Deccan trap lava of Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh.

questions.q: Which soil develops cracks in the dry season and is called ‘self-ploughing’?
questions.why: Black soil swells when wet and shrinks and cracks when dry, which aerates it.

questions.q: Laterite soil is formed by:
o: leaching under high temperature and heavy rainfall
questions.why: Heavy rain washes away silica and lime, leaving iron and aluminium oxides; such soil is used for making bricks.

questions.q: Red soil gets its colour from:
questions.why: Iron oxides in the crystalline rocks from which it forms give it a red colour.

questions.q: Deep, narrow channels cut by running water, as in the Chambal valley, are a result of:
questions.why: Gullies widen into ravines that make land useless for farming.

long.q: State three characteristics of alluvial soil and name two crops grown on it.
scheme: B1: it is formed by deposits of rivers and is found mainly in the northern plains and coastal deltas
B1: it is very fertile, rich in potash and lime but poor in nitrogen and humus
B1: it is of two types: khadar (new, light-coloured, renewed every year) and bhangar (old, darker, with kankar)
B1: crops: rice, wheat, sugarcane, jute (any two)

long.q: State three characteristics of black soil and explain why it is suitable for cotton.
scheme: B1: it is dark in colour, clayey and sticky when wet
B1: it is rich in iron, lime, magnesium and alumina, but poor in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter
B1: it develops cracks when dry and is self-ploughing
B1: it retains moisture for a long time, which suits cotton grown in areas of moderate rainfall

long.q: Distinguish between red soil and laterite soil on two points.
scheme: B1: red soil forms from weathering of ancient crystalline rocks such as granite under low rainfall; laterite forms by leaching in areas of high temperature and heavy rainfall
B1: red soil is light and porous and can be made fertile with fertilisers; laterite is acidic, poor in nutrients, and hardens on exposure to air, so it is used for bricks

long.q: State three causes of soil erosion.
scheme: B1: deforestation, which removes the plant cover that holds soil
B1: overgrazing by animals, which leaves the soil bare
B1: heavy rain and floods on slopes, strong winds in dry areas, and faulty farming methods such as shifting cultivation

long.q: Suggest four methods of soil conservation.
scheme: B1: afforestation and planting shelter belts of trees to check wind erosion
B1: contour ploughing and terrace farming on hill slopes
B1: building check dams and plugging gullies to control running water
B1: strip cropping, crop rotation and controlled grazing

questions.q: Tropical evergreen forests grow in areas with rainfall of more than:
questions.why: They need heavy rain and high temperature, as on the Western Ghats, in the north-east and the Andamans.

questions.q: Teak and sal are the main trees of:
questions.why: These forests, with 100-200 cm rain, shed their leaves in the dry season and give valuable timber.

questions.q: The Sundarbans are famous for:
o: mangrove forests with the sundari tree
questions.why: The tidal forests of the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta are named after the sundari tree; they are home to the Royal Bengal tiger.

questions.q: Babul, kikar and cacti grow in:
o: the dry areas of Rajasthan and Gujarat
questions.why: Tropical thorn and desert vegetation grows where rainfall is below about 70 cm.

questions.q: The Chipko movement (1973) was started to:
o: protect trees from being cut down
questions.why: Villagers in the Garhwal Himalayas hugged trees to stop commercial felling.

long.q: State three characteristics of tropical evergreen forests.
scheme: B1: they grow in areas of heavy rainfall (over 200 cm) and high temperature, such as the Western Ghats, the north-east and the Andaman Islands
B1: trees are very tall and dense, with a thick canopy, and do not shed their leaves all at the same time, so the forests stay green
B1: they give hardwood such as rosewood, ebony and mahogany, but are difficult to exploit because of dense undergrowth and mixed species

long.q: Explain why tropical deciduous forests are economically the most important forests of India.
scheme: B1: they cover a large area of the country, in regions of 100-200 cm rainfall
B1: they give valuable timber such as teak, sal, shisham and sandalwood
B1: trees of one species often grow together and the forests are less dense, so they are easier to exploit and transport

long.q: Describe the mangrove (tidal) forests and state two of their uses.
scheme: B1: they grow in the deltas of rivers such as the Ganga, Mahanadi, Godavari and Krishna, flooded by tides
B1: trees have breathing roots that stick out of the mud, and can live in salty water
B1: use: their wood is used as fuel and timber, and they provide habitat for wildlife such as the Royal Bengal tiger
B1: use: they protect the coast from erosion, storm surges and cyclones

long.q: State four measures for the conservation of forests.
scheme: B1: afforestation and reforestation of cut areas
B1: social forestry and agro-forestry, planting trees on village common lands and farm boundaries
B1: controlled felling and checking forest fires and grazing
B1: involving local people through Joint Forest Management and movements such as Chipko, and creating protected areas

long.q: State two ways in which forests are important to people.
scheme: B1: they provide timber, fuelwood and products such as lac, resins, gum, cane and medicinal plants
B1: they prevent soil erosion and floods, maintain rainfall and the oxygen balance, and give shelter to wildlife

questions.q: Tank irrigation is most common in:
o: Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh
questions.why: The hard rocky surface, seasonal rivers and uneven land make tanks the best way to store rainwater in the south.

questions.q: Which irrigation method uses pipes to deliver water drop by drop to the roots of plants?
questions.why: Drip irrigation wastes very little water and suits dry areas and orchards.

questions.q: Which state was the first to make rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for all buildings?
questions.why: Tamil Nadu made it compulsory in the early 2000s to recharge falling groundwater.

questions.q: Underground tanks built in houses in Rajasthan to store rainwater are called:
questions.why: Tankas store rainwater from rooftops for drinking; kuls are channels in Himachal, eris are tanks in Tamil Nadu, johads are earthen check dams.

questions.q: Tube wells are most widely used for irrigation in:
questions.why: The soft alluvium and high water table of the northern plains, with electricity, make tube wells easy to sink.

long.q: Give three reasons why irrigation is necessary in India.
scheme: B1: rainfall is seasonal, falling mainly in three or four months, so crops need water in the dry months
B1: rainfall is uneven in distribution and uncertain: some areas get little rain, and the monsoon may fail or break
B1: some crops such as rice and sugarcane need much water, and irrigation allows more than one crop a year (multiple cropping)

long.q: Why is tank irrigation popular in South India? Give three reasons.
scheme: B1: the rocky surface of the plateau does not allow rainwater to sink in, and digging wells or canals is difficult
B1: most rivers are seasonal and the land is uneven, with natural hollows that can be used as tanks
B1: settlements are scattered, and small tanks built by communities can serve each village

long.q: State two advantages and two disadvantages of canal irrigation.
scheme: B1: advantage: perennial canals supply water throughout the year to large areas
B1: advantage: once built, the cost of irrigation is low and canals also carry silt that adds fertility
B1: disadvantage: over-irrigation raises the water table and causes waterlogging and salinity (reh/kallar)
B1: disadvantage: seepage wastes much water, and stagnant water breeds mosquitoes

long.q: What is rainwater harvesting? Describe two methods used in India.
scheme: B1: rainwater harvesting is collecting and storing rainwater, or allowing it to recharge the groundwater, for later use
B1: rooftop harvesting: rain falling on roofs is led through pipes into tanks or recharge pits
B1: traditional methods such as tankas (underground tanks) and khadins in Rajasthan, or johads (small earthen check dams)

long.q: State two reasons why water must be conserved in India.
scheme: B1: groundwater levels are falling fast due to over-use for irrigation and in cities
B1: the growing population, industries and agriculture need more water, while many rivers and sources are polluted

questions.q: The best quality iron ore, with the highest iron content, is:
questions.why: Magnetite has up to about 72% iron; haematite, the most widely mined in India, has about 60-70%.

questions.q: Neyveli in Tamil Nadu is known for:
questions.why: Lignite, a low-grade brown coal, is mined at Neyveli and used in thermal power stations.

questions.q: India's oldest oil field is at:
questions.why: Oil was found at Digboi in Assam in the late 19th century; Mumbai High is an offshore field found in 1974.

questions.q: India's first nuclear power station was set up at:
questions.why: Tarapur in Maharashtra began working in 1969.

questions.q: Which is a non-conventional source of energy?
questions.why: Wind, solar, tidal, geothermal and biogas are renewable, non-conventional sources.

long.q: Name the four types of coal and state one feature of each.
scheme: B1: anthracite: the best quality, with the highest carbon content (over 80%); burns with little smoke
B1: bituminous: the most widely used; good for coking in iron and steel
B1: lignite: brown coal with lower carbon and high moisture, e.g. Neyveli
B1: peat: the first stage in coal formation, with low carbon and much smoke

long.q: Name one important mining area each for (a) iron ore in Jharkhand, (b) manganese, (c) bauxite in Odisha.
scheme: B1: (a) Singhbhum (Noamundi)
B1: (b) Balaghat (Madhya Pradesh) / Keonjhar (Odisha) / Bhandara and Nagpur (Maharashtra)
B1: (c) Koraput / Kalahandi

long.q: State two advantages of hydel power over thermal power, and one disadvantage.
scheme: B1: hydel power uses running water, a renewable resource, while thermal power burns coal, which will run out
B1: hydel power does not pollute the air, and dams can also give irrigation and flood control
B1: disadvantage: large dams are costly, flood forests and villages and displace people, and power output falls in dry years

long.q: Why is it important to develop non-conventional sources of energy in India? Give three reasons.
scheme: B1: conventional sources such as coal and petroleum are limited and will be used up
B1: burning fossil fuels causes air pollution and global warming; non-conventional sources are clean
B1: India has plenty of sunshine, wind and biomass, and these sources can supply power to remote villages, while reducing costly oil imports

long.q: Name two places in India for each: (a) wind energy, (b) geothermal energy.
scheme: B1: (a) Muppandal (Tamil Nadu) / Kachchh (Gujarat) / Jaisalmer (Rajasthan) (any two)
B1: (b) Puga valley (Ladakh) / Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh) (both)

questions.q: Which of these is a rabi crop?
questions.why: Rabi crops are sown in October-December and harvested in March-April; rice, cotton and jute are kharif crops.

questions.q: Shifting cultivation in the north-east of India is called:
questions.why: Farmers clear a patch of forest by slash and burn, farm it for a few years and then move on.

questions.q: Which state is the leading producer of tea in India?
questions.why: Assam's well-drained slopes, warm humid climate and heavy rain suit tea; Karnataka leads in coffee.

questions.q: Cotton grows best in:
o: black soil with about 210 frost-free days
questions.why: Cotton needs warmth, moderate rain, sunshine at picking and moisture-retaining black soil.

questions.q: The process of soaking jute stalks in water to separate the fibre is called:
questions.why: Jute stems are retted in slow-moving water; ginning separates cotton fibre from seeds.

long.q: Distinguish between kharif and rabi crops, with two examples of each.
scheme: B1: kharif crops are sown with the onset of the south-west monsoon (June-July) and harvested in September-October
B1: examples: rice, maize, cotton, jute, groundnut (any two)
B1: rabi crops are sown in winter (October-December) and harvested in spring (March-April)
B1: examples: wheat, barley, gram, mustard (any two)

long.q: State the climatic and soil conditions needed for growing rice.
scheme: B1: high temperature, above about 25 °C during the growing season
B1: heavy rainfall of over 100 cm, or irrigation where rain is less, as the fields must be flooded
B1: fertile clayey or alluvial soil that can hold water, as in river valleys and deltas

long.q: Describe the conditions required for growing tea and explain why tea is grown on hill slopes.
scheme: B1: tea needs a warm, moist climate, with temperatures of about 20-30 °C and rainfall of 150-300 cm spread through the year
B1: it needs deep, fertile, well-drained soil rich in humus and iron
B1: it is grown on hill slopes because water must not collect around the roots; slopes give good drainage
B1: plantations need plenty of cheap labour, since plucking (‘two leaves and a bud’) is done by hand

long.q: State two problems of Indian agriculture and suggest one remedy for each.
scheme: B1: problem: small and scattered land holdings make modern farming difficult
B1: remedy: consolidation of holdings and cooperative farming
B1: problem: dependence on an uncertain monsoon
B1: remedy: expansion of irrigation and water harvesting / crop insurance

long.q: What was the Green Revolution? State one of its results.
scheme: B1: the Green Revolution was the rapid rise in food-grain production in the 1960s, especially of wheat, from the use of high-yielding variety seeds with fertilisers, irrigation and machines
B1: result: India became self-sufficient in food grains / Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh gained most, increasing regional inequality

questions.q: Which of these is an agro-based industry?
questions.why: Agro-based industries use raw materials from farms: sugarcane, cotton, jute.

questions.q: The Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) is located at:
questions.why: It was set up in 1907 at Jamshedpur (Jharkhand), near the Subarnarekha and Kharkai rivers.

questions.q: The Bhilai steel plant was set up with the help of:
questions.why: Bhilai (Chhattisgarh) and Bokaro were Soviet-aided; Rourkela was West German and Durgapur British.

questions.q: Bagasse, a by-product of the sugar industry, is used for:
questions.why: The crushed cane fibre is burnt in the mill's boilers and used to make paper and board.

questions.q: Bengaluru is often called the ‘Silicon Valley of India’ because of its:
questions.why: It has many electronics and IT firms and research institutions.

long.q: Why is the sugar industry shifting from north India to peninsular India? Give three reasons.
scheme: B1: sugarcane in the south has a higher sucrose content because of the tropical climate
B1: the crushing season is longer in the south, so mills work for more months
B1: cooperative sugar mills in Maharashtra and Karnataka are well organised, and yields per hectare are higher

long.q: Name the raw materials needed for the iron and steel industry, and explain why Jamshedpur is a good location for it.
scheme: B1: raw materials: iron ore, coking coal, limestone and manganese (also dolomite and water)
B1: iron ore is available nearby from Singhbhum and Mayurbhanj, and coal from Jharia and Raniganj
B1: water from the Subarnarekha and Kharkai rivers
B1: cheap labour from nearby states and a rail link to the port of Kolkata for exports and markets

long.q: Why is Mumbai an important centre of the cotton textile industry? Give three reasons.
scheme: B1: it is near the cotton-growing black soil areas of Maharashtra and Gujarat
B1: it is a major port for importing machinery and exporting cloth, and has good rail links
B1: the humid climate suits spinning, and capital, labour and markets are readily available

long.q: State three uses of petrochemical products.
scheme: B1: plastics for packaging, pipes and household goods
B1: synthetic fibres such as nylon and polyester for clothing
B1: synthetic rubber, fertilisers, detergents, paints and medicines

long.q: Distinguish between public sector and private sector industries, with one example of each.
scheme: B1: public sector industries are owned and run by the government, e.g. the Bhilai Steel Plant (SAIL)
B1: private sector industries are owned and run by individuals or companies, e.g. TISCO (Tata Steel) at Jamshedpur

questions.q: The first passenger train in India ran in 1853 between:
questions.why: It ran on 16 April 1853 from Bori Bunder (Bombay) to Thane, about 34 km.

questions.q: The Golden Quadrilateral highway network links:
questions.why: It joins the four metropolitan cities; the North-South and East-West corridors link Srinagar-Kanyakumari and Silchar-Porbandar.

questions.q: National Waterway 1 is on the river:
questions.why: NW-1 runs on the Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly from Prayagraj to Haldia; NW-2 is on the Brahmaputra.

questions.q: Which mode of transport is the most suitable for carrying heavy, bulky goods over long distances on land at low cost?
questions.why: Railways carry large loads such as coal, ores and food grains cheaply over long distances.

questions.q: Which railway runs along the western coast through Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka?
questions.why: The Konkan Railway, completed in 1998, crosses many rivers and tunnels in the Western Ghats region.

long.q: State two advantages and two disadvantages of road transport.
scheme: B1: advantage: roads give door-to-door service and can reach hilly and remote areas
B1: advantage: they are cheaper to build than railways and good for short distances and perishable goods
B1: disadvantage: road transport is costly for heavy goods over long distances
B1: disadvantage: it causes congestion, accidents and air pollution, and many roads are damaged in the rains

long.q: Why are railways important for India's economy? Give three reasons.
scheme: B1: they carry bulky goods such as coal, iron ore, food grains and cement cheaply over long distances
B1: they carry millions of passengers daily at low fares, linking all parts of the country
B1: they help industry and trade, link ports to the interior, and help in times of famine and emergency

long.q: State three advantages and one disadvantage of air transport.
scheme: B1: it is the fastest mode of transport over long distances
B1: it can reach places difficult to reach by land, such as the north-east, mountains and islands
B1: it is useful for carrying perishable and valuable goods and for relief work in disasters
B1: disadvantage: it is very expensive, and is affected by bad weather such as fog

long.q: Why is inland water transport not well developed in India? Give two reasons.
scheme: B1: most rivers, especially in the peninsula, are seasonal, with little water in the dry season
B1: silting, waterfalls and rapids, and the diversion of water for irrigation, make rivers shallow and unsuitable for large boats

long.q: Name three major ports of India and state one feature of each.
scheme: B1: Mumbai: a large natural harbour on the west coast, handling much of India's trade
B1: Kolkata-Haldia: a riverine port on the Hooghly, needing constant dredging; Haldia was built to handle larger ships
B1: Visakhapatnam: the deepest land-locked, protected harbour on the east coast / Kandla (Deendayal): tidal port in the Gulf of Kachchh / Mormugao: exports iron ore from Goa

questions.q: Which of these is biodegradable waste?
questions.why: Biodegradable waste is broken down by microorganisms; plastic, glass and metal are not.

questions.q: Burning waste at very high temperatures in a closed furnace is called:
questions.why: Incineration reduces the volume of waste and is used for hospital (biomedical) waste.

questions.q: The Swachh Bharat Mission was launched on:
questions.why: It was launched on Gandhi Jayanti, 2 October 2014, to make India clean and free of open defecation.

questions.q: Using earthworms to convert organic waste into manure is called:
questions.why: Earthworms feed on organic waste and produce nutrient-rich vermicompost.

questions.q: The Bhopal gas tragedy of 1984 was caused by the leak of:
questions.why: Methyl isocyanate leaked from the Union Carbide pesticide plant, killing thousands; it shows the danger of industrial hazards.

long.q: State three sources of solid waste, with one example of waste from each.
scheme: B1: domestic: kitchen waste, paper, plastic packaging
B1: industrial: fly ash, slag, chemical sludge, metal scraps
B1: agricultural: crop stubble, animal dung / biomedical: used syringes, bandages / electronic: old phones and computers (any one)

long.q: Explain four harmful effects of improper disposal of waste.
scheme: B1: heaps of garbage breed flies, mosquitoes and rats, which spread diseases such as cholera, dengue and plague
B1: rainwater seeping through waste dumps carries harmful chemicals into the soil and groundwater
B1: burning of waste releases smoke and poisonous gases, polluting the air
B1: plastic waste blocks drains, causing waterlogging and floods, and harms animals that eat it

long.q: Why is segregation of waste at source important?
scheme: B1: separating wet (biodegradable) waste from dry waste lets the wet waste be composted easily
B1: dry waste such as paper, plastic, glass and metal can be sent for recycling
B1: it reduces the amount of waste going to landfills and keeps hazardous waste apart for safe disposal

long.q: Explain the ‘3 Rs’ of waste management with one example of each.
scheme: B1: Reduce: use fewer things that create waste, e.g. carry a cloth bag instead of taking plastic bags
B1: Reuse: use things again, e.g. using glass jars to store food
B1: Recycle: process used materials into new products, e.g. old newspapers made into recycled paper

long.q: Distinguish between dumping and sanitary landfill as methods of waste disposal.
scheme: B1: dumping is throwing waste in open low-lying areas, which causes foul smell, disease and pollution of water
B1: a sanitary landfill is a lined pit where waste is spread in layers and covered with soil, which reduces pollution and allows the land to be reused later
